title: Sharp Chest Pain Eased by Leaning Forward / Fever Changes Who Goes Home

blocks.text: Sharp Chest Pain Eased by Leaning Forward / Fever Changes Who Goes Home

AMaC MRCP PACES · X-20 · Consultation · PACES Consultation (Station 5) · Skills A, B, C, D, E, F, G · 20 minutes (15 with the patient, then 5 of examiner questions; warning at 13 minutes) · Guidelines: 2025 ESC Guidelines for the management of myocarditis and pericarditis (Eur Heart J 2025;46(40):3952-4041; online 29 August 2025) · Related AMaC: None identified
Dear Doctor, a 23-year-old university student. Four days of sharp central chest pain after a cold. It is worse lying flat and on deep breaths. Please assess and advise.
The patient has consented to see you. Please take a history, perform a relevant examination and explain your assessment and plan to the patient.

sections.heading: 4. The Hook and the Examiner Trap

blocks.text: The Hook. Sharp chest pain that is worse lying flat and eased by sitting forward after a viral illness is acute pericarditis. The marks come from the risk features that decide admission, and from knowing the first-line drugs.

The Examiner Trap. She feels well enough to go home. Candidates give ibuprofen and discharge without checking for fever, an effusion or tamponade. Pass: criteria, risk features, admission, ibuprofen and colchicine. Fail: discharged as low risk.

Say
Do
Ask about the pain, then the fever, the illness before it, drugs and any other heart or immune disease.
"What does the pain feel like? What eases it? Any fever, breathlessness or palpitations? Any recent infection?"
Pain pattern; fever; onset; breathlessness; viral illness; immunosuppression; trauma; anticoagulants; pregnancy.
Check the pulse, blood pressure, neck veins and chest, and listen for a rub.
"May I check your pulse, blood pressure and neck, and listen to your heart sitting forward? Tell me if anything hurts."
Pulse; blood pressure; paradox; neck veins; rub; chest; liver; ankles; cover her.
Explain the diagnosis, why the fever means hospital, and the drugs and warning signs.
"I think the lining of your heart is inflamed. Because of the fever I'd like to admit you."
ECG; echo; bloods; ibuprofen; colchicine; admission; tamponade signs.

Focused examination
Omits blood pressure or neck veins; reports a rub that is absent.
Finds a fever, a rub with the patient sitting forward, normal blood pressure and neck veins, and no pulsus paradoxus.
Also finds clear lung bases and no ankle oedema.
R4
D
Diagnosis and criteria
Calls it a muscle strain or a heart attack with no reasoning.
Acute pericarditis: typical pleuritic pain plus more than one supporting finding (rub, ECG changes, raised CRP, new or worse effusion).
Also separates it from myocardial infarction and pulmonary embolism, and names myopericarditis.
R5
E
Risk features and tests
Names no risk features; asks for no ECG or echo.

Names the major high-risk features of ESC 2025: fever above 38 °C, subacute onset, large effusion, tamponade and no response to anti-inflammatories after a week; asks for ECG, echo and blood tests including troponin.
Also names the minor features: myopericarditis (suggested by a raised troponin), immunosuppression, trauma and oral anticoagulation.
R6

Treatment and safety
Critical fail (AMaC practice flag, not an official automatic PACES fail): discharges her with a fever and no warning about tamponade.
Admits her, starts ibuprofen 600 mg three times daily with gastric protection and colchicine 0.5 mg daily (her weight is under 70 kg), and warns about breathlessness and faintness.
Also gives the duration, 1 to 2 weeks for ibuprofen and at least 3 months for colchicine, and the weight rule for colchicine.

Her concerns
Brushes aside her fear of a heart attack and of missing exams.
Asks what worries her, acknowledges both and explains this is usually treatable.
Also discusses her exams and her parents, and offers a letter for the university.

Tells her what to do with no choices.
Explains admission with a clear reason, asks her agreement and what she needs from home.
Records her choice, gives a written plan and a dated review.

blocks.text: High-performance is an AMaC teaching label, not an official grade. It shows what lifts a pass from adequate to convincing. Critical fail is an AMaC practice flag for an action that could harm the patient today; it is not an official automatic PACES fail.
Who you are: A 23-year-old student. You are anxious, short of time and worried about exams.
Opening line: "I've had this stabbing chest pain since last week. I think it's just a pulled muscle, but my flatmate made me come."
Volunteered: the pain is worse lying down and on deep breaths. It is better sitting forward. You had a cold two weeks ago.
Only if asked: you have felt feverish. No palpitations. You feel a little breathless. You take the contraceptive pill and nothing else. Your weight is 58 kg.
Only if asked about other illness: none. No blood thinners. No recent injury. You do not smoke; a little alcohol at weekends; no allergies; no recent travel; the only family history is your uncle.
Hidden concern (only if asked what worries you): you are afraid of a heart attack, like your uncle. Say: "My uncle died of a heart attack at 40."
Your questions, in your own words: "Is it my heart?" "Can I go back to the exam hall?" "Do I have to stay in?"
How you react: if told to stay in with no reason, you resist. If listened to and given the reason, you agree. If offered options, you choose.

Findings, released when examined: unwell but comfortable; respiratory rate 18; pulse 96 regular; blood pressure 118/74; SpO2 98% on air; temperature 38.4 °C. No pulsus paradoxus. Jugular venous pressure not raised. A scratchy rub heard at the left sternal edge, loudest sitting forward. Chest clear. No ankle oedema.
Results, only when requested: ECG: widespread concave ST elevation with PR depression. Echo: a small pericardial effusion, normal function. CRP raised. Troponin normal.

Question ladder: 1. What is the diagnosis and on what criteria? (D) 2. Which findings make her high risk? (E) 3. First-line drugs? (E) 4. What would suggest tamponade? (E) 5. What causes constriction later? (E)

Curveballs: She asks to go home to revise: not with a fever. She asks if it is a heart attack: normal troponin and widespread changes point to pericarditis. She becomes breathless and faint: suspect tamponade, urgent echo.
Introduces self, asks consent and asks about discomfort before examining (G)
Asks about posture, fever and the recent virus (C)
Checks blood pressure, neck veins and listens for a rub sitting forward (A)
Finds a rub, fever and no tamponade (B)
Names acute pericarditis from typical pain plus supporting findings (D)
Names fever above 38 °C as a high-risk feature (E)
Asks for ECG, echo and blood tests (E)
Starts ibuprofen with gastric protection and colchicine (E)
Warns about tamponade and admits her (E)
Asks what worries her and addresses her fear of a heart attack (F)
Fail performance
CANDIDATE: Lie flat. [R1 Fail] Muscle pain? [R2 Fail]
CANDIDATE: (Skips the blood pressure and neck.) [R3 Fail] A pulled muscle. [R4 Fail] No tests. [R5 Fail]
CANDIDATE: Take ibuprofen and go home. [R6 Fail] Nothing to worry about. [R7 Fail] Come back in a month. [R8 Fail]

Examiner note: Critical fail (AMaC practice flag, not an official automatic PACES fail): fever with pericarditis is a high-risk feature, and tamponade needs a warning. No consent, no examination, and the diagnosis missed.
Pass performance
CANDIDATE: I'm the registrar. May I check your pulse, blood pressure and neck and listen to your heart sitting forward? Tell me if anything hurts. I'll cover you afterwards. [R1 Pass]
CANDIDATE: What eases the pain? Any fever, breathlessness, or recent infection? Any tablets or other illness? [R2 Pass]
PATIENT: Sitting forward. I've felt feverish, and I had a cold.
CANDIDATE: (Examines.) A rub sitting forward, a temperature, normal blood pressure and neck veins, and no pulsus paradoxus. [R3 Pass]
CANDIDATE: I think this is acute pericarditis: the pain, the rub and the ECG changes. [R4 Pass]

CANDIDATE: Fever above 38 degrees makes you high risk, as would a large effusion, tamponade, a slow onset or no response to anti-inflammatories after a week. I'd like an ECG, an echo and blood tests including a troponin. [R5 Pass]

CANDIDATE: I'd admit you, start ibuprofen 600 milligrams three times a day with stomach protection and colchicine 0.5 milligrams once a day, and tell you to say at once if you're breathless or faint. [R6 Pass]
CANDIDATE: What worries you most? [R7 Pass]
PATIENT: A heart attack, like my uncle.
CANDIDATE: That is fair; your troponin is normal, so this looks like inflammation. [R7 Pass] Are you happy to come in? [R8 Pass]
Examiner note: Named pericarditis and the high-risk fever, and admitted her. Did not separate pericarditis from infarction or embolus, name myopericarditis, or give the durations and the weight rule.
High-performance performance
CANDIDATE: I'm the registrar. May I examine you? Would you like a chaperone? I'll ask about pregnancy only with your permission. [R1 High]
CANDIDATE: Any injury, blood thinners or previous tuberculosis? [R2 High]
CANDIDATE: (Examines.) Clear lung bases and no ankle swelling. [R3 High]
CANDIDATE: Pericarditis, not infarction or embolus; the troponin decides if the muscle is involved. [R4 High]
CANDIDATE: Minor risk features are myopericarditis, which a raised troponin would suggest, weak immunity, injury and blood thinners. [R5 High]
CANDIDATE: Ibuprofen 600 milligrams three times a day for one to two weeks; colchicine 0.5 milligrams daily at your weight for at least three months. [R6 High]
CANDIDATE: I'll write to your university. [R7 High]
CANDIDATE: I'll give you a written plan and a review date. [R8 High]
Examiner note: Added a chaperone, other causes, minor risk features, doses and durations, a letter for university and a written plan.
R2: Not asking about fever. A fever above 38 °C makes her high risk and decides admission.
R4: Calling it a pulled muscle. Pain eased by leaning forward after a virus is pericarditis.
R5: Ordering no echo. A large effusion or tamponade changes the plan.
R6: Discharging with a fever and no warning signs. Tamponade can develop.
"Can I ask about fever and what eases the pain?"
"The pain eases when you sit forward, so I'd say pericarditis."
"I'd like to check I've understood what worries you most."

ESC 2025: a definite diagnosis of acute pericarditis needs typical pleuritic chest pain plus more than one supporting finding: a pericardial rub, ECG changes, raised CRP, a new or worsening effusion, or CMR evidence of inflammation.

Admit if one or more high-risk features are present. Major features (ESC 2025): fever above 38 °C, subacute onset, large effusion (over 20 mm), tamponade, and no response to aspirin or an NSAID after at least 1 week. Minor features: myopericarditis (check troponin), immunosuppression, trauma and oral anticoagulation, which also raise concern. A patient with none who responds to anti-inflammatories can be managed as an outpatient.

First-line: aspirin 750 to 1000 mg every 8 hours or ibuprofen 600 mg every 8 hours (up to 800 mg) for 1 to 2 weeks then taper, with gastric protection (a proton pump inhibitor); add colchicine 0.5 mg once daily if under 70 kg, 0.5 mg twice daily if 70 kg or more, for at least 3 months. Check BNF and local protocol. Colchicine is not listed in the BNF for pericarditis (off-label use), so check the dose with local protocol or pharmacy.
THINK: Pain eased by leaning forward: pericarditis.
SAY: "The lining of your heart is inflamed."
DO: Ask about fever; listen to the heart sitting forward.
NUMBERS: High fever (above 38 °C): admit; colchicine at least 3 months (ESC 2025).
TRAP: Discharged as low risk; no tamponade warning.
FINISH: ECG, echo, ibuprofen, colchicine, admit.

Schulz-Menger J, Imazio M, et al. 2025 ESC Guidelines for the management of myocarditis and pericarditis. Eur Heart J 2025;46:3952-4041. https://doi.org/10.1093/eurheartj/ehaf192 Supports: diagnostic criteria, high-risk features (fever above 38 °C, subacute onset, large effusion, tamponade, no response to an NSAID; minor features), admission of high-risk patients, anti-inflammatory therapy and colchicine duration.
